ingredients.item: firm tofu, cut into 1 cm slabs, patted dry, salted lightly and rested 10 minutes
toasted sesame seeds ; a pinch of gochugaru , optional
/2 Korean radish, sliced into thin half-moons , the traditional bed — optional but excellent

instructions.heading: Step 1
instructions.action: The sear: oil at medium-high, slabs in without touching, 3–4 minutes to deep gold (they release when ready — nudged early, they tear), flip once, 2–3 minutes more, out to a plate.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: both faces evenly golden-brown with a firming surface — the crust is the sponge that will drink the braise; a pale slab stays bland no matter how good the sauce.

instructions.heading: Step 2
instructions.action: Pour off the oil, braise liquids into the pan (water, soy, honey, garlic), radish bed if using, seared slabs back over. Simmer 4–5 minutes at medium-low, spooning the liquid over the slabs twice.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the liquid has reduced to a glossy shallow pool and the slabs' faces have gone from dry-gold to lacquered amber; the tofu, pressed thin before, has visibly drunk.

instructions.heading: Step 3
instructions.action: Sesame oil off the heat, sesame and scallion over.
instructions.visualOrTactileCue: the eating test: a slab on rice — savory-sweet glaze, the crust's chew, the soft interior, and the radish (if used) sweet enough to surprise. It should taste like the banchan board's quiet centerpiece, which at a table full of grilled meat is exactly what it is.

storageNotes: Keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat in the pan 2 minutes with a splash of water. Cold glazed slabs in a lunchbox with rice are a Korean cafeteria staple by right.
Variations: gochugaru-dusted braise for the red bowl; the same braise over mushrooms and tofu together; a slice of cheese melted on the hot slab is the school-lunch fork — fusion, labeled, beloved.
